title: Creative and Game Writing
description: Learn how stories work and how to write them, from character and scene to dialogue and point of view, then apply the same craft to games with branching and reactive narrative.
audience: A capable adult who reads fiction or plays story-driven games and wants to write their own. Comfortable writing sentences; no creative-writing training assumed. Some basic comfort with if-then logic helps in the last third, but programming is not required.
outcomes: You'll be able to explain why a sequence of events becomes a story, and state a protagonist's want, obstacle and change.
You'll be able to compare three-act, five-part and four-part story structures and place events in them.
You'll be able to build a character from want, need, flaw and choices under pressure.
You'll be able to shape a scene around a goal, a conflict and a turning point.
You'll be able to write dialogue with subtext and distinct voices, and choose a point of view on purpose.
You'll be able to sketch a branching structure, count its writing cost, and track state with variables.
You'll be able to write game text that works for players: barks, quest text and interface strings.

modules.title: The shape of a story
modules.summary: What turns events into a story, how stories are structured, and who is in them.

modules.title: Scene and sentence
modules.summary: Writing the scene as a unit, then dialogue, point of view and revision.

modules.title: Writing for games
modules.summary: What changes when the reader acts: agency, branching structure, state, game text and consequence.

lessons.title: Want, obstacle, change
lessons.objective: Say what separates a story from a list of events, and state a protagonist's want, obstacle and change in three sentences.

concepts.title: Story and plot
concepts.summary: A story is events in time order; a plot links them by cause, so the second event happens because of the first.

concepts.title: Want
concepts.summary: A want is what a character is trying to get in the story, and it gives events a direction.

concepts.title: Obstacle
concepts.summary: An obstacle is whatever stands between the character and the want, and it makes the effort cost something.

concepts.title: Change
concepts.summary: A change is a difference between the character's situation or belief at the start and at the end.

concepts.title: Stakes
concepts.summary: Stakes are what the character stands to lose if the want fails.

misconceptions: Thinking a story needs a villain: the obstacle may be a place, a fear, time, or the character's own belief.
Thinking a plot is a series of exciting events: events without cause are only a sequence, however exciting.
Thinking change means the character becomes happier: it means different, and the change may be a loss.
sequence: Put two lists side by side: events in order, and the same events joined by 'because'.
Use Forster's example: 'The king died and then the queen died' is a story in his sense, and 'the queen died of grief' is a plot because the second event has a cause.
Name want, obstacle and stakes as the three things that supply the cause.
Look at a one-paragraph summary of a familiar story and mark the three parts.
Add change as the test of whether the story has ended.
examples: 'The king died and then the queen died' against 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief' (Forster, 1927).
Cinderella: wants to go to the ball; the obstacle is her stepmother's rule; stake is her place in the house; change is a new household.
A game example: Link wants to rescue Zelda; the obstacle is Ganon; the change is the fall of Ganon.

figures.shows: Two timelines of the same six events: one in plain order, one with causal arrows between events.
figures.learnerAction: Add arrows between events to convert a sequence into a plot.

figures.shows: A three-column table of want, obstacle and change for four short story summaries, one row left blank.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the blank row for a story the learner chooses.

questionPlan.sample: Which of these is a plot, in Forster's sense?
questionPlan.answer: The king died, and then the queen died of grief.
choices: The king died, and then the queen died.
The king died, and then the queen died of grief.
The king and the queen were old.

questionPlan.sample: In a story where a runner wants to win a race but has a broken ankle, what is the obstacle?
Write a three-sentence summary of a story you know: want, obstacle, change. Rate how confident you are that each part is present.
questionPlan.answer: self-rated: 1 to 5 on each of want, obstacle, change

historyNotes: E. M. Forster gave the king-and-queen example in Aspects of the Novel (1927), a series of lectures delivered at Cambridge in 1927.

lessons.title: Story structure
lessons.objective: Compare three-act, five-part (Freytag) and four-part (kishotenketsu) structures and place events within them, extending the arcs and turning scenes met in the English course.

concepts.title: Beginning, middle and end
concepts.summary: Aristotle's Poetics defines a whole as having a beginning, a middle and an end, each following necessarily from what came before.

concepts.title: Three-act structure
concepts.summary: Three-act structure divides a story into setup, confrontation and resolution; in a screenplay the acts are conventionally about 25, 50 and 25 percent.

concepts.title: Freytag's pyramid
concepts.summary: Freytag's five parts are exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe (denouement).

concepts.title: Kishotenketsu
concepts.summary: Kishotenketsu has four parts: ki (introduction), sho (development), ten (twist) and ketsu (conclusion), and does not depend on conflict.

concepts.title: The hero's journey
concepts.summary: Joseph Campbell described a recurring departure, initiation and return pattern in myth, which Christopher Vogler later reduced to twelve stages for film.

misconceptions: Treating structure as a formula that guarantees a good story: it is a description of patterns, not a recipe.
Believing every story needs conflict between characters: kishotenketsu builds interest from a twist in perspective.
Believing the climax is the last scene: in Freytag's model it is the middle of the pyramid, and the falling action follows.
sequence: Recall the arc and the turning scene from 'Structure: arcs and turning scenes' in the English course in a few lines, then widen the question: what other shapes can a story have?
Present Aristotle's whole and the three-act proportions with the percentages.
Draw Freytag's pyramid and fit a well-known story to it.
Show kishotenketsu with a four-panel example and explain how the twist re-reads the first panels.
Close with the hero's journey as a pattern in myth and say what it leaves out.
examples: A 120-page screenplay: act one ends near page 30 (25 percent), act two near page 90 (75 percent).
Freytag: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe: five parts.
Kishotenketsu: ki, sho, ten, ketsu: the twist is the third part.

figures.shows: A story timeline with beats from a short public-domain tale, positions marked as percentages.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each beat onto the three-act, Freytag and four-part grids to compare.

figures.shows: Freytag's pyramid with five labelled regions and a four-panel kishotenketsu row.
figures.learnerAction: Switch views.

questionPlan.sample: In a 120-page screenplay with act two beginning at 25 percent, on which page does act two begin?
In kishotenketsu, which of the four parts introduces the twist?
Which of these is the correct order of Freytag's parts?
questionPlan.answer: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe
choices: exposition, climax, rising action, falling action, catastrophe
exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe
rising action, exposition, climax, catastrophe, falling action
climax, exposition, rising action, falling action, catastrophe

historyNotes: Gustav Freytag published Die Technik des Dramas in 1863; Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces in 1949; Christopher Vogler's twelve-stage memo and book The Writer's Journey date from the 1980s and 1992.

lessons.title: Character
lessons.objective: Build a character from want, need, flaw and a defining choice, and say what a choice under pressure shows that description cannot.

concepts.title: Want and need
concepts.summary: A want is what the character pursues; a need is what the character must come to see or do to change, and the two often conflict.

concepts.title: Flaw
concepts.summary: A flaw is a habit or belief that works against the want, and it explains why the obstacle is hard for this character.

concepts.title: Choice under pressure
concepts.summary: A character is revealed by what they choose when the choice costs them.

concepts.title: Agency
concepts.summary: A character has agency when the events of the plot follow from their decisions.

concepts.title: Contradiction
concepts.summary: Specific contradictions, such as a generous miser, make characters feel like people.

misconceptions: Describing a character with traits ('brave, funny') and calling that characterisation: traits are claims, and choices are evidence.
Giving a character a tragic backstory and calling that depth: backstory explains, but depth comes from present choices that cost.
Making the character do what the plot needs: when events happen to a character, the character has no agency.
sequence: Introduce a character in two ways: with an adjective list and with one decision under pressure.
Define want, need and flaw with one worked character.
Show how contradictions give specificity.
Define agency and test it: which plot events could the character have prevented?
Try the exercise: write one choice that costs the character something they care about.
examples: A thief who wants money but needs trust: when offered a bigger score that would betray her partner, she turns it down.
Compare 'Mara is brave' with 'Mara went back for the dog while the roof was coming down.'
A game character: a mercenary who wants pay but keeps stopping to help strangers.

figures.shows: A character sheet with want, need, flaw, contradiction and defining choice; two examples filled in, one blank.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the blank sheet for a character of the learner's choice.

figures.shows: A branching decision with a cost on each branch.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a branch to see which trait it reveals (after the learner answers).

questionPlan.sample: Which sentence gives the best evidence of a character's courage?
questionPlan.answer: She went back into the burning shed for the dog.
choices: She went back into the burning shed for the dog.
She had no fear of heights.

questionPlan.sample: A hero is rescued at the climax by an unrelated stranger. Which quality is missing?
Write a want, a need and a flaw for a character you invented, then one costly choice. Rate how clearly the choice shows the flaw.

lessons.title: The scene
lessons.objective: Build a scene around a goal, a conflict and a turning point, and enter and leave it at the right moments.

concepts.title: Scene goal
concepts.summary: A scene goal is what the point-of-view character wants right now, small enough to be won or lost in the scene.

concepts.title: Scene conflict
concepts.summary: Conflict is the resistance to that goal, from another character, the situation or the character's own hesitation.

concepts.title: Turning point
concepts.summary: A turning point is the moment the situation changes direction, so the scene ends differently from how it began.

concepts.title: Outcome
concepts.summary: A scene outcome is usually a failure or a success with a cost, which pushes the next scene.

concepts.title: Enter late, leave early
concepts.summary: Start the scene as close to the conflict as possible and end it as soon as the turn has landed.

misconceptions: Thinking a scene is a place or a time: it is a unit of change in goal, conflict and outcome.
Thinking scenes should resolve what they raise: a good outcome often makes the problem larger.
Opening with arrival and small talk: the reader needs to meet the conflict early, and arrival belongs outside the scene.
sequence: Take a scene that works and list its goal, conflict and outcome.
Name the turning point with a value that flips (safe to unsafe, trusted to doubted).
Show how Swain splits writing into scene (goal-conflict-disaster) and the reaction that follows.
Cut a draft scene by moving its start to the first line of conflict.
Practise with a self-rated one-page scene.
examples: A scene in which a cook asks the owner for a raise: goal, a raise; conflict, the owner has just lost money; turning point, the owner offers the cook a share of the restaurant instead; outcome, success with a cost.
A scene starting with 'Maya sat down and said she was leaving' rather than with ten lines of greeting.
A value shift: the scene starts with hope and ends with doubt.

figures.shows: A scene drawn as a horizontal bar with a value line (positive to negative) and the turning point marked.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the turning point to the correct line of a sample scene before the answer is shown.

figures.shows: A draft scene with the opening lines struck out as a cut.
figures.learnerAction: Choose where the scene should begin.

questionPlan.answer: the demand to finish a month early
choices: the demand to finish a month early

questionPlan.sample: Which opening line best follows 'enter late'?
questionPlan.answer: 'You lied to me,' she said, setting the key on the table.
choices: Maya walked into the room and sat down.
'You lied to me,' she said, setting the key on the table.

questionPlan.sample: Write one page: a scene with a goal, a conflict and a turning point. Rate each of those three as clear or not.

lessons.title: Dialogue
lessons.objective: Write lines that carry subtext, give speakers distinct voices and avoid exposition that both speakers already know.

concepts.title: Subtext
concepts.summary: Subtext is meaning beneath what is said, so a line can mean more than its words.

concepts.title: Voice
concepts.summary: Characters differ in vocabulary, rhythm, sentence length and what they avoid saying.

concepts.title: Tags and beats
concepts.summary: A tag attributes a line ('she said'); a beat is an action between lines that shows what the speaker is doing or feeling.

concepts.title: Expository dialogue
concepts.summary: Dialogue where characters tell each other what both already know, only to inform the reader, reads as false.

concepts.title: Compression
concepts.summary: Real speech is full of filler; dialogue on the page keeps what the scene needs.

misconceptions: Thinking dialogue should sound like real speech: real speech has repetitions and false starts that page dialogue removes.
Thinking more adverbs and varied tags add life: 'said' is nearly invisible, and the line itself should carry the feeling.
Thinking characters should say what they feel: people often avoid it, and the avoidance is the drama.
sequence: Compare 'I'm angry that you forgot my birthday' with 'You're busy. I understand. Don't worry about it.' and say what changes.
Introduce subtext as a gap between what is said and what is meant.
Show how to build voices from vocabulary and rhythm with one line written for three speakers.
Explain tags and beats and where to place them.
Show a version of 'As you know, Bob' and rewrite it so the information comes out through conflict.
examples: The same request, 'Pass the salt', written by a child, a retired sergeant and a nervous host.
'Don't worry about it' as an expression of hurt.
A tag-free exchange with beats: she straightened the cutlery; he looked at the door.

figures.shows: A two-column page: spoken lines on the left, intended meaning (hidden) on the right.
figures.learnerAction: Select what the character means for each line.

figures.shows: Three characters and one situation, with a space for each character's version of one line.
figures.learnerAction: Write the three versions.

questionPlan.sample: Which line is the clearest example of an exposition dump?
questionPlan.answer: 'As you know, Bob, we have been business partners for ten years.'
choices: 'As you know, Bob, we have been business partners for ten years.'

questionPlan.sample: Which reply carries the most subtext when a friend asks 'Did you like the gift?'
choices: 'Yes, I love it, thank you so much.'

questionPlan.sample: Write one line asking for a lift to the airport in the voice of three different characters. Rate how different the three sound.

lessons.title: Point of view
lessons.objective: Choose a point of view for an effect, including second person and present tense for interactive text, building on 'Who sees and who speaks' in the English course.

concepts.title: First person
concepts.summary: First person tells the story as 'I', limited to what the narrator knows, perceives and chooses to say.

concepts.title: Second person
concepts.summary: Second person addresses 'you', common in interactive fiction because the reader acts.

concepts.title: Close third
concepts.summary: Close third uses 'he' or 'she' but stays inside one character's perceptions at a time.

concepts.title: Omniscient
concepts.summary: An omniscient narrator can enter any character's mind and describe events the characters cannot see.

concepts.title: Unreliable narrator
concepts.summary: An unreliable narrator tells the story in a way the reader learns not to trust.

misconceptions: Thinking first person means the narrator tells everything: the narrator knows only what they know, and can be wrong.
Mixing perspectives inside a scene (head-hopping) without realising: the reader loses track of whose mind they are in.
Thinking tense and person are the same choice: past or present tense is independent of person.
sequence: Recall the idea of narrator and focus from 'Who sees and who speaks' in the English course, then take one event told in four ways and compare what each version can say.
Define each point of view by the pronoun and by what the narrator can know.
Give the effect of each: intimacy, distance, irony or suspense.
Show unreliability with a narrator whose details do not match each other.
Link to games, where 'you' lets the player's choices be the narrator's.
examples: 'I locked the door and slept badly.' (first person)
'You lock the door and sleep badly.' (second person)
'Tom locked the door and told himself he was safe.' (close third) versus 'Tom did not know the window was open.' (omniscient)

figures.learnerAction: Place the narrator for a short passage.

figures.shows: Same event in four versions, with the information each version knows.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the blanks.

questionPlan.sample: 'You lock the door and sleep badly.' Which point of view is this?

lessons.title: Detail, subtext and revision
lessons.objective: Replace general statements with specific detail and revise a draft in three passes: structure, scene, then line.

concepts.title: Specific detail
concepts.summary: A specific detail is a concrete, sensory and chosen thing that implies a general truth without stating it.

concepts.title: Showing and telling
concepts.summary: Telling states a conclusion; showing gives evidence from which the reader draws it, and a good story uses both.

concepts.title: Revision passes
concepts.summary: Revise in order from largest to smallest: structure, scene, then line, because fixing sentences in a scene that will be cut wastes effort.

concepts.title: Cutting
concepts.summary: Most drafts improve when cut by a fifth to a quarter, removing repeats and restated points.

concepts.title: Reading aloud
concepts.summary: Reading aloud exposes rhythm problems that silent reading skips.

misconceptions: Thinking 'show, don't tell' means never summarise: summary is right for what does not matter much to the story.
Thinking more detail is better: detail must carry meaning, and each unneeded detail dilutes the one that matters.
Starting revision with sentence polish: sentences in a scene that will be cut are wasted work.
sequence: Show a flat sentence ('The kitchen was messy') and a specific version ('Three days of plates leaned against the tap').
Define specific detail and explain that it implies.
Place show and tell: show what matters, tell what does not.
Walk through three revision passes on a short draft.
Give cutting numbers: a 1,200-word scene cut by a quarter is 900 words.
examples: 'Three days of plates leaned against the tap' for 'The kitchen was messy'.
A 1,200-word scene cut by 25 percent is 900 words.
Reading a paragraph aloud and finding a sentence that makes you take a breath mid-clause.

figures.shows: A paragraph with highlight bands for 'telling' and 'showing' sentences.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each sentence as telling or showing before the key appears.

figures.shows: A three-pass revision checklist: structure, scene, line, with questions for each.
figures.learnerAction: Tick the questions answered for the learner's own draft.

questionPlan.answer: 'Three days of plates leaned against the tap.'
choices: 'Three days of plates leaned against the tap.'
'There was a lot of washing up.'

questionPlan.sample: A 1,200-word scene is cut by 25 percent. How many words remain?

lessons.title: Narrative in games
lessons.objective: Explain how a player's agency changes what narrative can do, and classify story delivery as embedded, enacted, evoked or emergent.

concepts.title: Player agency
concepts.summary: Player agency is the ability to make choices that matter to the game's events.

concepts.title: Four narrative types
concepts.summary: Henry Jenkins (2004) described evoked, enacted, embedded and emergent narrative: stories that rely on prior knowledge, stories the player performs, stories placed in the world, and stories that arise from play.

concepts.title: Ludonarrative dissonance
concepts.summary: Ludonarrative dissonance, a term from Clint Hocking (2007), is a conflict between what the story says and what the mechanics reward.

concepts.title: Environmental storytelling
concepts.summary: Environmental storytelling puts story in the arrangement of the world, such as a room that shows what happened there.

concepts.title: Cutscene and gameplay
concepts.summary: Cutscenes give the writer control, and gameplay gives the player control; good game writing moves between the two.

misconceptions: Thinking game stories are just films with interaction: the player can fail, skip, repeat and act, so the writer designs a structure, not a sequence.
Thinking more choices always means better story: each choice multiplies the writing, and unclear choices frustrate.
Thinking dialogue and cutscenes are the only places to tell story: level layout, items and mechanics tell too.
sequence: Start with a question: when you play a story-driven game, what tells you the story, and who is in control at that moment?
Name Jenkins's four types with an example of each.
Explain ludonarrative dissonance with Hocking's argument about BioShock.
Show environmental storytelling with a room and a set of objects.
Summarise the writer's problem: tell a story while the player is free to act.
examples: Embedded: a journal found on a shelf. Enacted: a stealth level the player performs. Emergent: a story the player tells about a strategy-game war.
A game in which the story says the hero values life while the mechanics reward killing every enemy.
A room with a child's bed, a locked door and a barricade: the story is in the layout.

figures.learnerAction: Drag examples into the right type.

figures.shows: A room layout with objects and a hover note on each.
figures.learnerAction: Order the objects to infer what happened.

historyNotes: Henry Jenkins published 'Game Design as Narrative Architecture' in 2004; Clint Hocking's blog post on BioShock dates from October 2007; Don Carson's article on environmental storytelling appeared in 2000.

lessons.title: Branching structures
lessons.objective: Draw and count the passages of common branching patterns, and choose a structure that fits a writing budget.

concepts.title: Branching
concepts.summary: Branching gives the player choices that lead to different passages.

concepts.title: Branching tree
concepts.summary: A branching tree never rejoins, so n binary choices give 2^n endings.

concepts.title: Branch and bottleneck
concepts.summary: In branch and bottleneck, branches rejoin at shared passages, which limits the amount of text.

concepts.title: Hub
concepts.summary: A hub structure returns the player to a central passage from several optional strands.

concepts.title: Writing cost
concepts.summary: The number of passages a structure needs, not its number of endings, is its writing cost.

misconceptions: Thinking that more branches always mean a richer story: unrestricted branching multiplies the work, and most branches get the least attention.
Thinking every choice must lead to a different ending: many choices change tone, information or relationships and then rejoin.
Counting only endings: the cost is the passages between.
sequence: Draw a single choice with two outcomes, then a second choice after each, and see the tree widen.
Count: 4 binary choices give 2^4 = 16 endings and 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 passages.
Show how a bottleneck turns the tree into a chain: each decision has its own short branches, then rejoins.
Present hubs and gauntlets from Ashwell's taxonomy.
Decide: given a budget, which structure is affordable?
examples: Four binary choices in a tree: 16 endings, 31 passages in all.
Three decisions with three options each, no rejoining: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 endings. With a bottleneck after each decision: 3 x 3 = 9 branch passages.
A hub of five strands, each of 3 passages, plus the hub: 16 passages.

figures.shows: Node-and-arrow diagrams of a tree, a bottleneck story, a hub and a gauntlet.
figures.learnerAction: Click nodes to count passages; the count display is hidden until the learner enters a number.

figures.shows: A branching tree growing level by level with the passage count on the right.
figures.learnerAction: Step down the levels.

questionPlan.sample: A story has 3 decision points with 3 options each and the branches never rejoin. How many different endings are there?
A branching tree has 4 binary choices with no rejoining. How many ending passages does it have?
A story has 3 decisions with 3 options each. After each decision the options each have one unique passage and then rejoin. How many unique branch passages are there in total?

lessons.title: State and conditions
lessons.objective: Use variables and conditions to make a story remember, and read a short script to say what it will show.

concepts.title: Variable
concepts.summary: A variable stores a value, such as a number, a true or false flag or a name, and can change as the story proceeds.

concepts.title: Flag
concepts.summary: A flag is a true-or-false variable recording that something happened.

concepts.title: Condition
concepts.summary: A condition tests a variable and decides which text appears or which choices are offered.

concepts.title: State space
concepts.summary: With n independent flags there are 2^n possible combinations, so tracked state grows quickly.

concepts.title: ink script
concepts.summary: In ink, VAR declares a variable, a line starting with ~ changes it, a line starting with * offers a choice, and { condition: A | B } shows A if the condition is true and B otherwise.

misconceptions: Thinking that a story with variables is a bigger tree: variables let one passage serve many histories.
Thinking more flags always add depth: unseen flags are writing cost with no reader effect.
Forgetting to initialise or reset a variable: a flag starts as false, and a counter starts at zero.
sequence: Show a one-room story that changes the same text depending on a trust number.
Define variable, flag and condition.
Read a short ink script line by line, tracking the variable.
Count the combinations of 3 flags: 2^3 = 8.
Decide which events deserve a flag: only those that something later will read.
examples: VAR trust = 0 / choice: Share your water / ~ trust = trust + 2 / gate: { trust >= 2: Mira unlocks the gate. | The gate stays locked. }
Choosing to keep walking leaves trust at 0, so the gate stays locked.
Three flags (met_mira, has_key, saw_fire) give 2^3 = 8 combinations.

figures.shows: A flowchart of a small script with a variable panel on the side that updates as the learner steps.
figures.learnerAction: Step the script and watch the variable.

figures.shows: The ink script as pseudo-code in a program trace, variables shown at each line.
figures.learnerAction: Step through.

questionPlan.sample:
In this ink script, what does the player see at the gate after choosing 'Share your water'?
VAR trust = 0
=== start ===
You meet Mira.
* [Share your water]
    ~ trust = trust + 2
    -> gate
* [Keep walking]
    -> gate
=== gate ===
{ trust >= 2: Mira unlocks the gate. | The gate stays locked. }
-> END
Using the same script, what does the player see at the gate after choosing 'Keep walking'?
A story tracks 3 independent true-or-false flags. How many combinations of flag values are possible?

lessons.title: Writing game text
lessons.objective: Write barks, quest text and interface strings that work in repeated, interrupted and translated play.

concepts.title: Bark
concepts.summary: A bark is a short line triggered by an event, such as a guard's 'Over here!'.

concepts.title: Repetition budget
concepts.summary: The number of distinct lines needed is the rate of play divided into the time, so that the player does not hear the same line twice in a window.

concepts.title: Quest text
concepts.summary: Quest text tells the player what to do and where, in as few words as possible, with story kept in the quest's reasons.

concepts.title: String limits and expansion
concepts.summary: Interface strings have length limits, and translation may lengthen them; a common allowance is about 30 percent for languages longer than English.

concepts.title: Interruptibility
concepts.summary: Lines must make sense when cut off, skipped, or heard out of order.

misconceptions: Writing game text like prose: text that works on a page can fail when it repeats, scrolls past or is cut off.
Forgetting that the player may skip: critical information goes in at least two places.
Hard-coding gender, number and word order: translated strings need variables and slack.
sequence: Take a combat bark and ask what happens the twentieth time it plays.
Compute a repetition budget: barks every 15 s over 10 minutes need 40 distinct lines to avoid repeats.

lessons.title: Choice, consequence and pacing
lessons.objective: Design choices that are distinct, understood and reactive, and plan a small branching vignette inside a word budget.

concepts.title: Meaningful choice
concepts.summary: A choice is meaningful when the options are clearly different, the player can predict something about their effects, and the game later responds.

concepts.title: Delayed consequence
concepts.summary: A delayed consequence shows the effect of an earlier choice in a later scene.

concepts.title: Reactive text
concepts.summary: Reactive text changes a few lines to acknowledge a choice, without a new branch.

concepts.title: Pacing
concepts.summary: Pacing in a branching story balances choice frequency with passage length, so the player is neither idle nor overloaded.

concepts.title: Word budget
concepts.summary: A word budget fixes how many words each shared and branching passage may use.

misconceptions: Offering choices whose options mean the same: that is the illusion of choice, and players notice it.
Confusing hidden consequence with fairness: if the player cannot predict anything about an option, the choice is a coin toss.
Writing every consequence as a new branch: a line of acknowledgement is often enough.

courseCheck: A mixed check of: telling a plot from a story and stating want, obstacle and change; placing events in three-act, Freytag and four-part structures; judging a choice as characterisation; locating a scene's turning point; spotting subtext and exposition in dialogue; identifying point of view; counting endings and passages in branching patterns; reading a short ink script; and budgeting barks, string lengths and vignette words. Several writing tasks are self-rated against clear criteria.
platformNeeds: A 'story_graph' figure type: nodes (passages) and edges (choices) with optional variable panel. The learner steps through a small story, sees state variables change and counts passages or endings. The svg_figure and program_trace fallbacks in lessons 9 and 10 stand in.

A 'code-run-ink' runner (or code-reading with an in-app ink player): inkjs is MIT-licensed and runs in the browser, which would let the learner edit and run short scripts and see the output. Lesson 10 uses code-reading questions until it exists.

A self-rated writing task type with a word counter, a saved draft and a rubric checklist, so the Q kind 'self' can show criteria (for example 'goal, conflict, turning point present') and store the learner's own rating. The learner's text should never be sent anywhere without consent.
A 'text_annotation' figure: highlight and label spans in a short passage (telling versus showing, point of view, tags and beats). A table or svg_figure with preset sentences is the fallback.
unverified: All source URLs: the research session had no outbound web access, so none of the sources were opened. Gutenberg ebook numbers, the archive.org links, Ashwell's blog URL, Hocking's URL, Jenkins's MIT URL and Carson's Gamasutra/Game Developer URL are from memory.
The ink syntax in lesson 10 (VAR, ~, *, [ ], -> and {cond: a | b}) is from memory of the ink documentation and was not run. A writer should compile the sample before use.

The dates for Aspects of the Novel (1927), Die Technik des Dramas (1863), Campbell's book (1949), Vogler's The Writer's Journey (1992), Jenkins (2004), Hocking (2007) and Carson (2000) are from memory.
The 25/50/25 screenplay split is a convention taught in screenwriting guides, not a rule; the lesson should present it as such. The 30 percent text expansion is a rule of thumb.
The kishotenketsu description (ki, sho, ten, ketsu) is standard but its use in Japanese game design (for example Nintendo level design) is from memory and not included in the plan.
